(a) Study Required.—
        (1) In general.—The Commission shall review and analyze the need for enhanced examination and enforcement resources for investment advisers. 
        (2) Areas of consideration.—The study required by this subsection shall examine—
            (A) the number and frequency of examinations of investment advisers by the Commission over the 5 years preceding the date of the enactment of this subtitle; 
            (B) the extent to which having Congress authorize the Commission to designate one or more self-regulatory organizations to augment the Commission’s efforts in overseeing investment advisers would improve the frequency of examinations of investment advisers; and 
            (C) current and potential approaches to examining the investment advisory activities of dually registered broker-dealers and investment advisers or affiliated broker-dealers and investment advisers.   
    (b) Report Required.—The Commission shall report its findings to the Committee on Financial Services of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs of the Senate, not later than 180 days after the date of enactment of this subtitle, and shall use such findings to revise its rules and regulations, as necessary. The report shall include a discussion of regulatory or legislative steps that are recommended or that may be necessary to address concerns identified in the study.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that this is only an internal Commission study with a report to congressional committees, which stays inside the federal government and would be "No". However, the section also directs the Commission to use its findings to revise its rules and regulations as necessary, which is a direction to engage in rulemaking, and the definition treats rulemaking as participation. The call is close because the rule revision is conditional ("as necessary") and no comment process is spelled out.
fable.s: shall use such findings to revise its rules and regulations, as necessary

opus.w: The section tells the Commission to revise its rules and regulations based on the study. Under the DEFINITION, requiring rulemaking counts as participation, and Example 6 counts it even when the agency has discretion. The tempting 'No' reading treats the section as only a study and a report to congressional committees, both of which stay inside the government. That reading misses the rulemaking clause, which is what brings outside parties in.
opus.s: shall use such findings to revise its rules and regulations, as necessary
opus.b:
**Step 1: The tempting reading and why it fails.** Most of this section is a study, plus a report to two congressional committees. Both stay inside the federal government, so on their own they would be a "No." But subsection (b) also tells the Commission it "shall use such findings to revise its rules and regulations, as necessary." The DEFINITION counts "requiring rulemaking" as a "Yes," and Example 6 counts even optional authority to regulate. Rulemaking brings in notice-and-comment, which involves the public. The "as necessary" qualifier makes this less certain, but per Example 6, discretion does not stop it from counting.

**Step 2: Label.**

qwen_chat.w: The section requires the Commission to conduct a study and report its findings to congressional committees. Congress is inside the federal government, so reporting to it is not participation. The section does not require consultation with any outside parties (states, tribes, public, experts) before making a decision, nor does it establish an advisory body with non-federal members. The mention of revising rules is an internal administrative action based on the study, not a participatory process defined in the text.
qwen_chat.s: The Commission shall report its findings to the Committee on Financial Services of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs of the Senate
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the Commission is required to "use such findings to revise its rules and regulations," this implies a rulemaking process that typically involves public comment. However, the text itself does not mandate public participation in the rulemaking; it only mandates the internal study and the reporting of findings to Congress. The definition requires that the section *itself* involve consultation or coordination with outsiders. Reporting to Congress is explicitly excluded ("Congress... are all INSIDE the federal government"). There is no mention of public hearings, advisory committees with non-federal members, or consultation with states/tribes/public in this specific text.
